title: Pick coverage
lead: Groundwork for predicting how two defenders play an on-ball screen: the label, what each call looks like in the tracking, when it becomes visible, what drives it, and the bar a model must beat.

blocks.text: Before training a model to predict how two defenders play an on-ball screen, this tab checks what the label is, how often each call happens, what each call looks like in the tracking, when it becomes visible, what it depends on and whether there is enough data. No model is fitted.

items.label: Picks
items.sub: on-ball screens in the ten games

items: SkillCorner labels every pick twice. **bhrDefType** is the ball handler's defender: over, under, switch, ice or blitz ('none' is documented but never used in these games). **scrDefType** is the screener's defender: soft, show, switch, ice, blitz or none
**Switch, ice and blitz are always called for both defenders together**, and over or under always pairs with soft, show or none. So the two fields are really one call with seven values
The seven joint calls match the rows of the coaching table: over · soft (drop), over · show (hedge), under · soft, under · show, switch, ice and blitz

blocks.text: Are the ten games typical of the season?

The season files count only direct picks (the handler or screener shot, assisted or was fouled right after) and only from the offense's side, so they give the league-wide mix of each call but not the joint call. The ten games' direct picks are compared with them.

blocks.title: Handler's defender: ten games vs season
Screener's defender: ten games vs season

items: Over · soft and over · show together are 66% of the calls; always guessing the commoner one is right 33% of the time

The season mix is close to the sample's: over 66%, under 15% and switch 18% of season direct picks. Only 2 of 22,085 season direct picks have no call on the handler's defender and 89 none on the screener's
Ice (1.0% of season direct picks) and blitz (0.3%) are rare league-wide, not just in this sample

sections.title: What each call looks like in the tracking

blocks.text: For every pick, the four players of the action are followed from 3 s before to 2 s after the pick frame. Lines are averages per joint call (blitz left out: 4 picks). The dashed line is the pick frame.

items: **Time 0 is the screen.** The handler passes closest to the screener a median 0.2 s after picks.frame (middle half 0.2 to 0.4 s)

**Level vs screen** = the player's distance to the hoop minus the screen spot's, in feet. Positive is above the screen (farther from the hoop), negative below it. Over keeps the handler's defender above, under takes him below; show brings the screener's defender up toward the ball, soft keeps him back
**Who is who.** ballhandlerDefId and screenerDefId name the defenders before any switch. The matchups table agrees on 95% of picks just before the screen

items: Under: the handler's defender is 3.1 ft below the screen 0.4 s after the pick; with over he is still 1.6 ft above it
Show: the screener's defender is 7.2 ft from the handler 0.4 s after the pick, against 10.1 ft for soft (both with over)
Switch: by +2 s the handler's own defender is 14.0 ft away and the screener's defender 5.5 ft
Under picks start higher: 1 s before the pick the handler is 10.8 ft above the screen on under · soft picks, 7.7 ft on over · show
The matchups table backs the switch label: 71% of switches hand the handler to the screener's defender, against 5% of over/under picks
Averages hide spread: single picks overlap a lot, which the next section measures
The ice lines rest on 14 picks

sections.title: When does the call become visible?

blocks.text: This decides what a model can honestly claim. If the calls only differ after the screen, a model that sees frames after time 0 is recognising the coverage, not predicting it.

items: **Separation (AUC).** Take one pick of each kind at random. The AUC is how often a measure puts them the right way round: 0.5 is a coin flip, 1 is always right. It is computed for one measure at one moment at a time
The charts show it for each measure from −3 s to +2 s, for three questions a model would face

items: Under or over is barely visible 1 s before the screen (best AUC 0.59) and nearly certain 0.4 s after it (0.97)
Show or soft shows earliest: the screener's defender's level separates 0.67 at −0.4 s and 0.84 at the pick frame
A switch shows last: best 0.64 at the pick frame, 0.85 at +1 s and 0.91 at +2 s

So a before-the-screen model has to lean on the defenders' set-up and on context, which alone says little (section 7). A model allowed to look 0.5-1 s past the screen is mostly reading a label already visible in the tracking
One measure at one moment is a floor: a model combining measures and frames will separate better, especially before the screen
SkillCorner's labels come from its own tracking model, so some of the after-screen separation is the labelling rule itself

items: **Defenses differ.** A defense's most common call covers 30% to 71% of its picks in a game, and the most common call itself changes from defense to defense

**No streaks.** A defense's call equals its previous call in the same game 31% of the time. If its calls in that game came in random order, the match rate would be 30%, so calls are not streakier than the defense's overall mix
The same screener's defender repeats his own previous call 32% of the time

The season files give, for every ACB player, the calls he faced as a handler and as a screener over 293 games. The coaching logic says defenders go under non-shooters and drop (soft) against rollers rather than poppers.

items: Each baseline predicts a pick's call from the shares of calls in a reference group, with one pick of each call added so nothing gets probability zero, and the league mix added with the weight of five picks
Groups built from games are built without the pick's own game (leave one game out). 'Earlier calls' and 'previous call' use only picks before this one in the same game

The season baseline multiplies the handler's season share of over, under, switch, ice and blitz by the screener's season share of show and soft, each pulled toward the league with the weight of 20 picks

**Accuracy** = how often the most likely call was right. **Log loss** = the average of minus the log of the probability given to the true call; lower is better, and guessing all seven calls equally scores 1.95

items: The bar from league shares alone: log loss 1.52. Its accuracy is only 26% because over · soft and over · show are nearly tied, so which one it picks flips from game to game
No honest look-up moves log loss by more than 0.02 (best: 'By shot-clock band', 1.50). Context alone says little about the call
Knowing a defense's whole-game mix (cheating, it includes the answer) would give 1.42: that is roughly the most a team-scheme prior could be worth
So the real signal must come from the tracking around the screen (section 3), which is the case for a sequence model
Ice (14) and blitz (4) cannot be learned from 1,514 picks; plan to merge or drop them

sections.title: What this means for a transformer

items: **Decide the task first.** Predicting from frames up to the screen is forecasting. Letting the model see 0.5-1 s past it is mostly recognising a call already visible in the tracking (section 3). Both are useful, but they answer different coaching questions

**Label.** Use the joint call. 2 of the seven have under 20 picks, so a practical version has five values (over · soft, over · show, under · soft, under · show, switch), or two heads (handler: over, under or switch; screener: soft, show or switch)

**Tokens.** One token per player per frame, with fixed roles for the four players of the action (handler, screener and their two defenders) plus the other six. Coordinates in the viewer frame (attacking +x, screen y corrected), possibly also relative to the screen spot

**Context.** The shot clock, how high the handler starts, and the handler's and screener's season shooting shift the mix, but only a little (section 7). The defense's earlier calls did not help. Context tokens are worth including, not worth relying on
**Never inputs.** bhrOutcomes, scrOutcomes, direct, and anything about the shot or points: all are recorded after the call
**Size.** 1,514 labelled picks, about 151 per game, with every defense but three seen in one game only. Split by game, report each held-out game, and compare against the baselines above

**Same lesson as the kickout model.** There a logistic model with a few good features tied the transformer. Fit the baselines and a small logistic model on hand-made features (the level and distance measures above) before the transformer
